Hippocrates

GeometryConstructionsCircles
Game: This picture shows an old way to cut an angle into three equal parts; the goal is to make the two marked dots meet.
How to play: Drag A, C or E, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick "Show names" and, once the dots meet, "Hint" to see why the split works.
Look for the math

An old trisection method uses a marked circle instead of just a ruler and compass. The trick is to choose E so that the length EH is twice the length AC; then the small angle at A is exactly one third of the big one. This page describes that construction; there is no score and nothing to lose.

Build the picture

Drop a line from C straight down to AB; its foot is D. The line through A parallel to CD meets the line through C parallel to AB at F, so ADCF is a rectangle and CE runs parallel to AB. The dashed circle is centred at E and has radius 2·AC. Point K lies on the line EA at that radius from E, and G is the midpoint of E and K. H is where AE crosses CD. The picture is finished when K and H are less than one drawing unit apart — the exact test used by the Java applet.

Why one third?

Let the big angle at A be θ and the small one φ. Because CE is parallel to AB, the angle at E is also φ. When K reaches H the length EH is 2·AC, so in the right triangle CEH the midpoint G of the hypotenuse is AC from C, E and H. That makes triangle CGE isosceles with base angles φ, so the outside angle at G is 2φ; triangle ACG is isosceles too, giving θ = φ + 2φ. Tick Hint at a match to see the marks.

What the page says, and what is true

The old page states plainly: when EH = 2·AC, ∠BAE = ∠BAC / 3. The logic test confirms this for every acute angle it tries (angles under 90°), to machine precision. It is not true without that restriction: with C to the left of A the angle BAC is obtuse and the same construction gives about 116.6° and 98.9°, a ratio near 1.18, not 3. The current page also says to put G on H, but the code compares K with H; at a match G is still half of EH away from H. The 2006 version of the page called the midpoint G, which agrees with the code. The Java applet is gone from the live page (it now embeds a GeoGebra construction); the original embedded Hippocrates.class is confirmed in the 2006 Internet Archive capture. This is a neusis construction, not a ruler-and-compass one.

Try dragging C upward, then use the left and right arrow keys on E (hold Shift for bigger steps) to bring the two coloured dots together again.
